newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia Yield Spreads-Looking to tighten further.
newsitem.headline: Australia Yield Spreads-Looking to tighten further.

text.p: The Australian/U.S. 10-year bond yield spread contracted to its lowest level for over a decade at one stage on Monday at just below 50 basis points and analysts generally see this trend continuing.

"I think you can see spreads come in much tighter. I don't think we'll sustain spreads below the U.S., but I think we're likely to see spreads in negative territory at some stage over coming months," Bruce Hockman, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, told Reuters Financial Television.
The 10-year margin has seen a dramatic contraction in just over a year, largely on the back of Australia's much improved inflation outlook, which now stands well below that of the U.S.
Australian annual headline inflation stood at 1.3 percent at the end of the March quarter compared with 2.5 percent in the U.S. at the end of April.

According analysts at Citibank Australia the spread at Monday's low was its lowest since 1981 and well before the financial markets were deregulated in the mid-1980s, but they noted that the local bond market was less sophisticated then.

The spread now stands over 200 basis points below that seen in April 1996, with the latest sustained push from 100 basis points in the past three weeks stemming from a run of weak data, not least last week's labour force data.

Expectations are running high that the Reserve Bank will cut current official interest rates at 5.5 percent sooner rather than later. The jury is still out as to whether the Federal Reserve will tighten in July, although recent data suggests the Fed may refrain, analysts said.
Friday's weak U.S. PPI helped the Australian 10-year yield breach of 7.0 percent on Monday to its the lowest level since February 1994.

The break of 65 basis points on the local spread to the U.S. after last week's jobs data now sets the market up for a test of 30 basis points in the near term, said Su-Lin Ong, fixed income economist at Hambros Bank.
"While the Aussie-U.S. spread may widen modestly towards the end of the year, the movement is likely to be limited unless the U.S. market turns particularly bearish," Ong added.

On the day, the market was only outperformed by the short-end of the Canadian curve within the dollar bloc, which took last Friday's U.S. data as further evidence that the Fed will leave policy on hold at the FOMC meeting on July 1/2.
